name: Republic of Austria
info: The Second Austrian Republic, re-established in 1945 after seven years inside Nazi Germany, remembered for a decade of Allied occupation, the State Treaty and perpetual neutrality of 1955 and its prosperity within the European Union.

facts.founder: Karl Renner, who with Adolf Schärf, Leopold Kunschak and Johann Koplenig declared Austria's independence from the Third Reich on 27 April 1945 and headed the provisional government as state chancellor
facts.predecessor: Austria as part of Nazi Germany (1938–1945: the Ostmark, from 1942 the Alpine and Danubian Reichsgaue); before the Anschluss the First Austrian Republic (1919–1934) and the Austrofascist state of Dollfuss and Schuschnigg

t: Austria's second republic was declared on 27 April 1945 with the approval of the Red Army, while most of the west and south were still under Nazi rule; the Federal Constitutional Law of 1920 was declared valid again on 1 May 1945.

The Austrian State Treaty of 15 May 1955 ended ten years of Allied occupation; on 26 October 1955, with the last troops gone, parliament declared the country's perpetual neutrality, and the day is now Austria's National Day.

After a referendum carried by two-thirds in 1994 Austria joined the European Union on 1 January 1995, signed the Schengen Agreement the same year and adopted the euro in 1999; Vienna hosts the OSCE and OPEC.
dyk: Austria built a nuclear power station at Zwentendorf on the Danube after a unanimous vote of parliament in 1972, then voted 50.5% to 49.5% against nuclear power in a 1978 referendum; parliament banned it and the finished plant never produced electricity.
ev: On 27 April Karl Renner, Adolf Schärf, Leopold Kunschak and Johann Koplenig declare Austria's secession from the Third Reich and set up a provisional government in Vienna, backed by Joseph Stalin.
On 26 July parliament passes the first nationalisation law; about 70 mining and manufacturing companies pass to the state.
The Austrian State Treaty of 15 May restores full independence; on 26 October, with the occupation troops gone, parliament declares permanent neutrality.
A referendum rejects nuclear power by 50.5% to 49.5% and the finished Zwentendorf plant is never switched on.
Kurt Waldheim, former secretary-general of the United Nations and a Wehrmacht officer accused of war crimes, is elected president.
Austria joins the European Union on 1 January after a two-thirds referendum majority, and signs the Schengen Agreement.
Sebastian Kurz's People's Party wins the snap election and forms a government with the Freedom Party, sworn in on 18 December; it falls in 2019 over the Ibiza scandal.
After the election of 29 September, coalition talks collapse and Karl Nehammer resigns; a People's Party, Social Democrat and NEOS coalition under Christian Stocker eventually takes office.

sections.foundation:
The republic declared in 1945 was Austria's second. The first, proclaimed as German-Austria in 1918 from the German-speaking lands of the fallen Habsburg monarchy and renamed by the Treaty of Saint-Germain, lasted until Engelbert Dollfuss shut down parliament in 1933; the Austrian Civil War of February 1934 outlawed the Social Democrats, and on 13 March 1938 the Anschluss made Austria a part of Nazi Germany. Under Nazi rule Jewish property was seized, the pogrom of November 1938 struck Vienna and other cities, and the Mauthausen camp and its sub-camps worked prisoners to death. Some 65,000 Jewish Austrians were murdered in the Holocaust, 140,000 had fled in 1938–39, and 260,000 Austrians died in the Wehrmacht.

Vienna fell to the Soviet offensive on 13 April 1945. On 27 April Karl Renner and Adolf Schärf of the Socialists, Leopold Kunschak of the Christian Socials and Johann Koplenig of the Communists declared Austria's secession from the Third Reich and set up a provisional government under Renner with the approval of the Red Army; the date is officially the birthday of the republic. On 1 May the constitution of 1920, abolished by Dollfuss in 1934, was declared valid again. The country was divided into four occupation zones under the Allied Commission for Austria, with the government in Vienna inside the Soviet zone, and was recognised by the Allies in October 1945. It was a landlocked alpine land of 83,879 square kilometres and nine states.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Second Republic began with nationalisation: on 26 July 1946 parliament took about 70 mining and manufacturing companies into state hands. Many of the largest firms stayed nationalised until the 1980s, after which privatisation brought state holdings down to the levels of other European economies. Austria built a highly industrialised social market economy in which labour organisations and the chambers of workers, business people and farmers weigh heavily, and it consistently ranks high in GDP per capita, today the 13th highest in the world. Germany has always been the main trading partner, which leaves Austria exposed to the German economy; at least 67% of imports come from other EU states, and membership from 1995 drew foreign investors seeking the single market and the economies to the east.

Austrian firms became consolidators in Eastern Europe after the fall of communism, announcing 4,868 mergers and acquisitions worth 163 billion euros between 1995 and 2010. International tourism is the most important sector beside industry, almost 9% of GDP, with 20.8 million arrivals in 2007. More than half of the electricity comes from hydropower and renewables supply 62.89%. The population reached 9.22 million in April 2026; 22.3% were foreign-born in 2024, mostly from the former Yugoslavia, Germany, Turkey and Romania, and growth to 10.18 million by 2080 is expected from immigration. Catholics, 74% in 2001, were about 50% in 2023.
sections.military:
The Second Republic has never fought a war, and its defence rests on the neutrality declared in 1955, by which Austria will join no military alliance and allow no foreign bases on its soil. The Austrian Armed Forces, the Bundesheer, rely on conscription: men found fit at eighteen serve six months followed by an eight-year reserve obligation, and women have been able to become professional soldiers since 1998. The army has about 26,000 soldiers, some 12,000 of them conscripts, organised in Joint Forces of land, air, international and special forces; as a landlocked country Austria has no navy. Defence spending was about 0.8% of GDP in 2012. The president is nominal commander-in-chief, the minister of defence exercises command.

Within its neutrality Austria has a tradition of UN-led peacekeeping and humanitarian missions, with larger contingents in Bosnia and Kosovo and the all-volunteer Austrian Forces Disaster Relief Unit, able to deploy in ten hours. After the fall of the Soviet Union it reassessed its stance, granting overflight rights for the UN-sanctioned action against Iraq in 1991, joining NATO's Partnership for Peace in 1995 only after Russia had, and taking part in the EU's Common Foreign and Security Policy; the ban on foreign bases is the only part of the 1955 law still fully in force. The army helped the border guards against illegal crossings from the Eastern bloc frontier until Hungary and Slovakia joined Schengen in 2008.
sections.governance:
Austria is a federal, representative democratic republic of nine states under the Federal Constitutional Law of 1920, amended in 1929 and re-enacted on 1 May 1945. The president, directly elected with a run-off, is head of state and selects the chancellor, who forms a government on the strength of the Nationalrat; that chamber of 183 seats is elected every five years by citizens over sixteen, the voting age lowered in 2007, and can dismiss the government by a vote of no confidence. The Constitutional Court invalidates laws that breach the constitution, the European Court of Justice has overruled Austrian decisions since 1995, and the European Convention on Human Rights is part of the constitution.

Politics was long governed by Proporz: important posts were shared between the Social Democratic Party (SPÖ) and the Austrian People's Party (ÖVP), and the chambers of interest groups were consulted on nearly all legislation. Single-party governments ruled only in 1966–1970 (ÖVP) and 1970–1983 (SPÖ); otherwise grand coalitions or small coalitions with a third party held office. From 2006 both big parties weakened as Jörg Haider's right-wing parties and later the Greens and NEOS grew; Sebastian Kurz governed with the Freedom Party from December 2017 and with the Greens from January 2020 until his resignation in a corruption scandal in October 2021, followed by Alexander Schallenberg, Karl Nehammer and, after the 2024 election, Christian Stocker.
sections.impact:
Neutral Austria made itself a meeting place. It joined the United Nations in 1955, is a founding member of the OECD and Interpol, and hosts the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Vienna, capital of the former multi-ethnic Habsburg Empire, kept its role as the city of Central Europe with the strongest ties east and south, and after the end of the Cold War Austrian banks and companies became leading investors in the former Eastern bloc. Membership of the European Union from 1995, the Schengen Agreement and the euro bound the country into the west, while the SPÖ and ÖVP still argue over whether neutrality or closer European defence, even NATO, should define it.

The republic also had to face its past. In 1992 Chancellor Franz Vranitzky officially acknowledged that thousands of Austrians had taken part in serious Nazi crimes. The Carinthian Slovenes and the Croats and Hungarians of Burgenland received minority rights under the State Treaty of 1955, and the Roma and Sinti were recognised in 1994. The loss of South Tyrol to Italy stayed a grievance before Italy granted the region wide autonomy. Austria's cultural weight continued: Herbert von Karajan led the Berlin Philharmonic for 35 years, the quantum physicists Anton Zeilinger and Peter Zoller followed Schrödinger and Pauli, and the country ranked 17th in the Global Innovation Index in 2024.
sections.decline:
The Second Republic's recent decades have been marked by the loosening of its two-party order. In the 2008 election the SPÖ fell to 29.3% and the ÖVP to 26.0%, while the Freedom Party and Jörg Haider's Alliance for the Future of Austria together approached 20%. The grand coalition broke in 2017, and Sebastian Kurz's ÖVP took 31.5% and governed with the Freedom Party until the Ibiza corruption scandal forced new elections in 2019; his coalition with the Greens, sworn in on 7 January 2020, lost him to another corruption scandal in October 2021, and Austria had three conservative chancellors in two months. After the election of 29 September 2024 talks between ÖVP, SPÖ and NEOS first collapsed, Karl Nehammer resigned, an ÖVP–FPÖ attempt failed, and the three parties finally formed the Stocker government.

The economy weathered the 2008 crisis with scars: the government bought the Hypo Alpe-Adria-Bank for one euro in 2009, and in 2014 Chancellor Werner Faymann warned that its failure would compare with the Creditanstalt collapse of 1931. Today the republic faces an ageing society, with an average age of 44.5 years in 2020, and a climate that has warmed almost 2 °C since 1880, bringing more heat waves, floods and landslides and shrinking glaciers and snow. It remains among the most prosperous and peaceful states in the world, neutral by law, a member of the European Union and host to international organisations in Vienna.

summary: The Second Austrian Republic was declared on 27 April 1945 as the Third Reich collapsed, regained full independence by the State Treaty of 1955 and declared perpetual neutrality that October. It grew into one of the world's richest states, joined the European Union in 1995 and the euro in 1999, and governs nine federal states from Vienna, host of the OSCE and OPEC.
references: Steven Beller, A Concise History of Austria (Cambridge University Press, 2006)
Barbara Jelavich, Modern Austria: Empire and Republic, 1815–1986 (Cambridge University Press, 1987)

pointDescs.1945: Austria's independence is declared on 27 April and the 1920 constitution restored on 1 May, under four Allied occupation zones.
pointDescs.1955: The State Treaty of 15 May ends the occupation; neutrality is declared on 26 October and Austria joins the United Nations.
pointDescs.1966: The first single-party government of the republic, the ÖVP's, takes office; the schilling and the social market economy are well established.
pointDescs.1978: The referendum against nuclear power leaves the finished Zwentendorf plant idle; the economy is highly industrialised with large nationalised firms.
pointDescs.1986: Kurt Waldheim is elected president; privatisation of the nationalised industries is beginning.
pointDescs.1995: Austria joins the European Union, Schengen and the Partnership for Peace and becomes a leading investor in post-communist Eastern Europe.
pointDescs.2006: Growth reaches 3.3% in the year the SPÖ emerges strongest from the October election: the republic's economic high point.
pointDescs.2008: The financial crisis hits; the Hypo Alpe-Adria-Bank is bought by the state for one euro in 2009 and both big parties lose ground.
pointDescs.2017: Sebastian Kurz's ÖVP wins the snap election and governs with the Freedom Party from 18 December.
pointDescs.2021: Kurz resigns in a corruption scandal on 11 October; Schallenberg and then Karl Nehammer follow within two months.
pointDescs.2024: The election of 29 September brings a long coalition crisis that ends in the Stocker government of ÖVP, SPÖ and NEOS.
pointDescs.2025: Austria is a prosperous, neutral EU member of 9.2 million people, with 22% of its residents foreign-born and an ageing population.

notes: The registered start 1945 is the Second Republic; the Habsburg monarchy, the First Republic and the Nazi years are kept to foundation and predecessor.
The article's Bibliography section is empty, so references is [].
The article gives no date for the formation of the Stocker government after the 29 September 2024 election; the event is dated 2024 by the election.
The peak of the curve (2006) rests on the article's growth figure of 3.3% for that year; the article gives no economic series, so the curve is a judgement.
Military figures (26,000 soldiers, 0.8% of GDP) are dated 2012 or undated in the article; Austria's defence spending today is not given.
